newsitem.title: CROATIA: IMF urges economic prudence on Croatia.
newsitem.headline: IMF urges economic prudence on Croatia.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) said on Tuesday Croatia would have to pursue a prudent economic policy to secure further financial backing through 1999.

"Targets are real economic growth of five percent or more which is necessary to create jobs...with a rate of inflation of 3-4 percent," Robert Feldman, the IMF chief of mission to Croatia, told a news conference.
He said a new arrangement -- an extended fund facility (EFF) -- to the tune of $450-500 million over the next three years was "contingent on achieving this programme".
The IMF and Croatian government have just agreed key measures to be enforced for the duration of the new loan, expected to be approved by the fund's board in spring 1997.
It will replace a previous stand-by arrangement which supported the government's efforts in curbing war-induced hyper-inflation and stabilising the kuna currency.
Feldman said it was essential for Croatia's future policies to focus on preserving a sound macroeconomic environment.
"People have a long memory of past inflation...If inflation were to start rising, it would get difficult to keep it within reasonable limits," he said.
Careful wage and fiscal policies, combined with the central bank's moves to boost international reserves, would create greater confidence in the currency and the economy in general.
In this way, the government would eliminate most inflationary pressure, Feldman added.

He said the government must press on with overhauling and privatising the banking sector to enable a better allocation of resources to support growth, which could only be financed by higher savings and investments.
Though some layoffs and labour redistribution may clearly be needed in certain cases, enterprises would also benefit from a further sell-off to make them more efficient and viable.
"Certainly, the IMF would welcome any other measures in this direction," Feldman said.
